input.strategy_title: Surface model deployment status in the RHOAI Dashboard
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Data scientists deploying models through the Dashboard cannot tell whether a
deployment is healthy without leaving the console. InferenceService state is
only visible via `oc get inferenceservice` or by reading Kubernetes events,
which most Dashboard users cannot access. Support cases regularly begin with
"my model has been Pending for an hour" — information the platform already has
but does not surface.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | Users see a deployment status (Ready, Progressing, Failed) for each deployed model in the Dashboard model serving views. |
| HLR-2 | P0 | Users can open a status detail view showing the underlying condition messages and recent events for a failed or progressing deployment. |
| HLR-3 | P1 | Displayed status reflects the actual InferenceService state within 30 seconds of a change, without a manual page reload. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | Users can filter and sort the deployed models list by status. |
| HLR-5 | P2 | Product documentation explains each status value and the first troubleshooting steps for Failed deployments. |

## Affected Components

- Dashboard
- KServe

## Out of Scope

- Alerting or notifications on status transitions
- Status history / timeline views
- ModelMesh deployments (KServe InferenceService only)

## Open Questions

None blocking — KServe already exposes the needed conditions on the
InferenceService status; this strategy is about surfacing them.

# Surface InferenceService deployment status in the Dashboard model serving views

## Description

This epic delivers deployment status visibility for KServe InferenceService
models directly in the RHOAI Dashboard, so data scientists can tell whether a
deployment is healthy without leaving the console or using `oc` commands. It
covers the status display in the model serving views, a status detail view
with underlying condition messages and recent events, automatic status
freshness, and filter/sort by status.

## Scope

- Display a deployment status — Ready, Progressing, Failed — for each deployed
  KServe InferenceService model in the Dashboard model serving views, derived
  from the InferenceService CR status conditions.
- Add a status detail view showing the underlying condition messages and
  recent Kubernetes events for a failed or progressing deployment.
- Ensure the displayed status reflects the actual InferenceService state
  within 30 seconds of a change, without a manual page reload. The refresh
  mechanism (polling interval vs. Kubernetes watch) is an implementation
  decision for the Dashboard team.
- Add filter and sort controls for the deployed models list by status.
- Scope is limited to KServe InferenceService deployments; ModelMesh
  deployments, alerting/notifications on status transitions, and status
  history / timeline views are out of scope per the strategy.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Each deployed KServe InferenceService shown in the Dashboard model serving
  views displays one of the statuses Ready, Progressing, or Failed, derived
  from the InferenceService status conditions.
- A user can open a status detail view for a failed or progressing deployment
  that shows the underlying condition messages and recent events.
- After a change in the actual InferenceService state, the displayed status
  reflects the new state within 30 seconds without a manual page reload.
- The deployed models list can be filtered by status and sorted by status.
- The condition-to-status mapping used by the Dashboard has been validated
  with the RHOAI Serving team against actual InferenceService conditions in
  both serverless and raw deployment modes.
- The Dashboard build and test pipeline passes with these changes.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): Users see a deployment status for each deployed model in the
  Dashboard model serving views.
- HLR-2 (P0): Users can open a status detail view showing the underlying
  condition messages and recent events for a failed or progressing deployment.
- HLR-3 (P1): Displayed status reflects the actual InferenceService state
  within 30 seconds of a change, without a manual page reload.
- HLR-4 (P2): Users can filter and sort the deployed models list by status.

# Validate KServe InferenceService status conditions for Dashboard consumption

## Description

This epic validates that the InferenceService status conditions and
Kubernetes events exposed by KServe are complete, stable, and accessible
enough for the RHOAI Dashboard to derive and surface deployment status
(Ready, Progressing, Failed). KServe requires no code changes for this
strategy; this is the serving team's validation of the passive component it
owns, producing an agreed condition-to-status mapping contract for the
Dashboard implementation.

## Scope

- Enumerate the InferenceService CR status conditions and related Kubernetes
  events in both serverless and raw deployment modes.
- Confirm the conditions are sufficient to derive each of Ready, Progressing,
  and Failed, including failure paths (for example, a predictor that fails to
  become ready), and identify any gaps.
- Confirm the condition messages and recent events needed by a status detail
  view are accessible with the permissions of typical Dashboard users.
- Produce an agreed condition-to-status mapping document for Dashboard
  consumption, covering both deployment modes.
- No KServe code changes are expected; if gaps are found, document them with
  a recommended fallback (for example, an alternate condition or event source)
  rather than fixing KServe in this epic.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A condition-to-status mapping covering both serverless and raw deployment
  modes exists and is agreed with the RHOAI Dashboard team.
- Each of Ready, Progressing, and Failed is derivable from the documented
  conditions, or any gap is documented together with a fallback the Dashboard
  can use.
- Representative failure scenarios (for example, a failed predictor rollout)
  are verified to produce conditions and events that the mapping classifies
  as Failed.
- The accessibility of status conditions and recent events for typical
  Dashboard user permissions is confirmed and documented.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0, validation): the deployment status shown by the Dashboard is
  derived from validated InferenceService status conditions.
- HLR-2 (P0, validation): the condition messages and recent events shown in
  the status detail view are validated as present and accessible.

# Document deployment status values and Failed-deployment troubleshooting

## Description

This epic delivers the product documentation for the new deployment status
surface in the RHOAI Dashboard: what each status value means and the first
troubleshooting steps a user should take for a Failed deployment. It is
authoring work only; it describes the capability after it is built and
validated.

## Scope

- New or updated product documentation topics covering:
  - each deployment status value (Ready, Progressing, Failed) and what it
    means for a deployed KServe InferenceService model;
  - where and how status is displayed in the Dashboard model serving views,
    including the status detail view with condition messages and recent
    events;
  - the first troubleshooting steps for a Failed deployment, based on the
    condition messages and events shown in the detail view;
  - filtering and sorting the deployed models list by status.
- Content must stay within strategy scope: no coverage of alerting,
  notifications, status history/timeline views, or ModelMesh deployments.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Published documentation explains each status value (Ready, Progressing,
  Failed) and where status is shown in the Dashboard.
- Published documentation provides first troubleshooting steps for Failed
  deployments, referencing the condition messages and events available in the
  status detail view.
- The documentation is technically reviewed against the implemented Dashboard
  behavior and the validated condition-to-status mapping; review sign-off is
  recorded.
- Documentation covers filtering and sorting the deployed models list by
  status.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-5 (P2): Product documentation explains each status value and the first
  troubleshooting steps for Failed deployments.

# Decomposition Summary — RHAISTRAT-9001

Strategy: Surface model deployment status in the RHOAI Dashboard

## Triage Outcome

Not below-threshold and not docs-only. The scope spans two distinct work
streams (Dashboard code implementation by RHOAI Dashboard, plus substantive
product documentation authoring for HLR-5) and two owning teams (RHOAI
Dashboard, RHOAI Serving for KServe validation), so a single-epic
decomposition does not apply and the full pipeline ran.

## Epic List

| ID | Title | Type | Team | Priority |
|----|-------|------|------|----------|
| RHAISTRAT-9001-E001 | Surface InferenceService deployment status in the Dashboard model serving views | Implementation | RHOAI Dashboard | P0 |
| RHAISTRAT-9001-E002 | Validate KServe InferenceService status conditions for Dashboard consumption | Implementation | RHOAI Serving | P0 |
| RHAISTRAT-9001-E003 | Document deployment status values and Failed-deployment troubleshooting | Implementation (docs-authoring) | RHOAI Documentation | P1 |

## Dependency DAG

```mermaid
graph TD
    RHAISTRAT-9001-E001 --> RHAISTRAT-9001-E003
    RHAISTRAT-9001-E002 --> RHAISTRAT-9001-E003
```

## DAG Justification

| Edge | Rule | Rationale |
|------|------|-----------|
| E001 ∥ E002 (no edge) | Rule 14 | Different repos (odh-dashboard vs kserve), no shared build artifact: the InferenceService CRD conditions already exist (per strategy and KServe architecture context), so the Dashboard implementation does not build against anything E002 produces. Coordination on the condition-to-status mapping is a review/AC gate on E001, not a DAG dependency. |
| E001 → E003 | Rule 11 | docs-authoring epic is blocked by every Implementation epic; documentation describes the status surface that was built. |
| E002 → E003 | Rule 11 | docs-authoring epic is blocked by every Implementation epic; the documented status semantics must reflect the validated condition mapping. |

## HLR Traceability Matrix

| HLR | Priority | Epic(s) |
|-----|----------|---------|
| HLR-1 (status shown per deployed model) | P0 | E001 (implementation), E002 (validation of the condition source) |
| HLR-2 (status detail view: conditions + events) | P0 | E001 (implementation), E002 (validation of the condition source) |
| HLR-3 (status fresh within 30s, no reload) | P1 | E001 |
| HLR-4 (filter/sort by status) | P2 | E001 |
| HLR-5 (product documentation for statuses and troubleshooting) | P2 | E003 |

All five HLRs are covered; no orphaned requirements.

## Decomposition Decisions

- **KServe is a passive component.** The strategy states KServe already
  exposes the needed InferenceService status conditions and open questions
  are "None blocking", so no KServe code changes are in scope. Because the
  passive component is owned by RHOAI Serving (a different team than the
  active Dashboard epic), the passive-component validation is a separate
  validation Implementation epic owned by RHOAI Serving (E002) rather than an
  AC on the Dashboard epic.
- **No Investigation epics.** The strategy explicitly declares no blocking
  open questions, and no conditional ADRs, pending reviews, or risks tables
  appear. The refresh mechanism for HLR-3 (polling vs. watch) is an
  implementation detail the Dashboard team resolves; it does not change which
  epics exist.
- **HLR-1 through HLR-4 stay bundled in E001.** HLR-3 (freshness) and HLR-4
  (filter/sort) are lower-priority HLRs, but they share the same UI surface
  (model serving views / deployed models list), the same status data derived
  from InferenceService conditions, and the same access path — splitting them
  would create two epics building the same surface plus an artificial
  serialization edge. They are captured as scope and acceptance criteria of
  the single Dashboard epic. E001 is the densest epic (four HLRs) and sits
  near the single-sprint upper bound for the Dashboard team; if it overruns,
  HLR-4 (filter/sort, the only P2 HLR on this surface and the thinnest
  increment) is the designated deferral — it is independent of the other
  three HLRs and can slip without affecting the P0 status display or detail
  view.
- **docs-authoring priority exception.** E003 derives P1 from the strategy
  frontmatter priority (Major → P1); it does not push priority onto E001/E002.
- **Component mappings.** Strategy lists "Dashboard" and "KServe" — both are
  verbatim canonical component names. HLR-5 implies the canonical
  "Documentation" component for E003 (not listed in the strategy's Affected
  Components; noted below as a health warning). No non-obvious mappings were
  needed.
- **Out of scope honored.** Alerting/notifications, status history/timeline
  views, and ModelMesh deployments are excluded from every epic's scope.

## Health Warnings

- **Missing strategy sections.** The strategy has no Impacted Teams table, no
  Dependencies table, no formal Given/When/Then acceptance criteria, and no
  Non-Functional Requirements section. Owning teams were inferred from the
  architecture context (`.context/architecture-context/architecture/rhoai-3.0/`):
  Dashboard → RHOAI Dashboard, KServe → RHOAI Serving. Epic acceptance
  criteria were derived from the HLRs and problem statement rather than from
  strategy ACs.
- **Affected Components list is incomplete.** HLR-5 requires product
  documentation, but "Documentation" is not listed among affected components.
  The decomposition adds the Documentation epic to guarantee HLR coverage.
- **HLR-3 freshness target is a soft NFR.** "Within 30 seconds without a
  manual reload" is the only timing requirement; the mechanism (polling
  interval vs. Kubernetes watch) is left to the implementing team, per the
  decompose-don't-design constraint.

## Tiered Delivery

Not applicable — no external dependency with uncertain timing; all work is
in-platform.

The bundling of HLR-3/HLR-4 into the P0 epic E001 passes the deferrability test — they share the same UI surface, the same condition-derived data, and the same access path — and the decomposition goes further by designating HLR-4 as the explicit in-epic slip, so lower-priority work cannot hold the P0 delivery hostage.

**2. Epic boundaries — solid.** Three distinct component/team tuples (Dashboard/RHOAI Dashboard, KServe/RHOAI Serving, Documentation/RHOAI Documentation), with team inference from architecture context honestly disclosed as a health warning. No duplication: E001 builds the UI surface, E002 produces the validation/mapping deliverable that E001 consumes (a producer/consumer relationship, not two epics independently building the same thing), E003 authors docs only. No code/docs mixing within any epic. E001 is the densest epic (four HLRs) and is self-identified as near the single-sprint upper bound, but it remains one surface, one sprint's scale, with a named deferral path — not a multi-sprint monolith.

**3. DAG quality — solid.** The Mermaid arrows (E001 → E003, E002 → E003) run dependency → dependent and exactly match E003's frontmatter `dependencies`; E001/E002 correctly have none. Both edges are Rule 11 docs-last edges, present and justified. The E001 ∥ E002 parallelism is the trickiest call and is handled well: different repos, no shared build artifact (the CRD conditions pre-exist per the strategy), with the one real coupling — the condition-to-status mapping — deliberately treated as an AC/review gate on E001 rather than a DAG edge. That is a defensible reading (E001 builds against the pre-existing CRD, not an E002 artifact), and the alternative (serializing E002 → E001) would have artificially serialized genuinely parallel-eligible work. Critical path 2 fits a small strategy.

**4. Scope fidelity — solid.** No invented API paths, CRD field names, env vars, caching policies, or response formats. The epics lean on exactly what the strategy supplies (Ready/Progressing/Failed, conditions, recent events, 30-second freshness) and explicitly delegate the one open implementation choice (polling vs. watch) to the implementing team. The KServe-side references to serverless/raw deployment modes and predictor failure paths are real domain concepts used to scope validation, not design inventions, and E002 explicitly refuses to fix KServe in-epic. Out-of-scope items (alerting, history, ModelMesh) are excluded in every epic. No epic body references sibling draft IDs; full IDs appear only in frontmatter, as required. E002 itself is a defensible reading of "KServe" as an affected component given the strategy's statement that KServe needs no code changes — and it matches the annotation's expected shape (KServe-side epic, Dashboard epic, docs last).

Acceptance criteria — solid.** Every AC is testable (status displayed per model, detail view contents, 30-second freshness without reload, filter/sort, mapping agreed, failure scenarios classified as Failed, permission accessibility confirmed, published docs with sign-off). Rule-mandated ACs are present where applicable: E003 carries the technical-review sign-off AC for docs-authoring; rollback/feature-flag is correctly N/A (new capability, not replacement); E001 includes a build/test pipeline AC even though no konflux chain exists. Notably, E002's permission-accessibility AC catches a real latent risk in the strategy (Dashboard users' ability to read events) rather than papering over it.

The only candidate deductions — E001's density, the AC-level coupling between E001 and E002, and the serverless/raw-mode validation scoping — are all judgment calls the decomposition explicitly reasons about, discloses, and defends, which is precisely what a strong decomposition should do. The output also matches the annotation's expectations (3 epics, no triage, both P0s traceable, docs last).
